title: Is LSU this good or is Clemson that bad? Either way, Lane Kiffin’s debut a rousing success
author: Matt Baker
content:
BATON ROUGE, La. — Lane Kiffin’s long-awaited, much-heralded LSU debut went about as well as anyone could have reasonably expected. After months of assorted drama, weeks of legal wrangling, days of chaotic uncertainty and even a two-hour weather delay, his No. 11 Tigers routed Clemson in a season-opening 51-10 win at Tiger Stadium.

LSU (1-0) got off to a shaky start when former Arizona State starter Sam Leavitt — one of the nation’s top transfer quarterbacks — threw an interception on a tipped pass on his team’s second play from scrimmage. Clemson’s ensuing field goal effectively ended the highlights for Dabo Swinney’s Tigers (0-1). LSU dominated from there, handing Clemson its most lopsided loss since 2000.

LSU rushed for 213 yards in the first half alone; the Tigers hadn’t totaled that many in a full game against a Power 4 opponent in more than two full seasons. Leavitt led the way with a pair of first-half touchdowns on the ground. LSU’s defense was equally stout. Clemson had minus-4 rushing yards and only one first down through two quarters. Swinney pulled new starting quarterback Christopher Vizzina late in the first half for freshman Tait Reynolds. It didn’t matter. LSU ultimately outgained Clemson 644 to 145.

The performance seemed like an early vindication for Kiffin, the $13-million-a-year lightning rod. LSU poached him from Ole Miss at the end of last regular season, Kiffin leaving the Rebels for a rival before the College Football Playoff. More recently, Kiffin pursued a pair of players who spent offseason time on NFL rosters. The ongoing legal spat spiked Thursday when the SEC sued him, LSU and two other Tigers officials.

“I think it’s overrated,” Kiffin said of the drama and its effects.

The results also feel like an early referendum for Swinney, who has lost four consecutive openers in which Clemson hasn’t scored more than 10 points. The two-time national champion went 7-6 last year as his Tigers have struggled to adapt to the NIL/transfer portal era.

If there was any wonder if Kiffin’s team would allow the cacophony around the coach and the roster situation to divert its focus from Saturday’s primary task, it was erased pretty quickly.

LSU was the better team by a mile, and that much was clear before halftime arrived. Leavitt used his athletic ability to give Clemson’s defense headaches and ran for two early touchdowns; he found receiver Winston Watkins Jr. and tight end Trey’Dez Green early and often; running back Dilin Jones chewed up yards on the ground; and Clemson didn’t have much of an answer for any of it.

Leavitt doesn’t appear to be suffering any lingering problems from the foot surgery he underwent last season at Arizona State. He was able to run around and be dynamic outside the pocket, which is what makes him such a fun watch and so hard to defend. A healthy Leavitt means LSU will have a chance whenever the Tigers have the ball.

Meanwhile, defensive coordinator Blake Baker did a good job of deploying the studs LSU has on that side of the ball, led by returning star linebacker Whit Weeks and transfers Princewill Umanmielen, Jordan Ross and TJ Dottery. The LSU front kept Vizzina from getting comfortable, and one well-timed, well-schemed blitz drawn up by Baker rattled Vizzina enough to force a poor throw that resulted in a 30-yard touchdown return by Ross.

If this was supposed to be a heavyweight battle, LSU won by TKO before it got to the middle rounds. — Sam Khan Jr.

Kiffin circled back to ESPN’s Holly Rowe and said it took everything for him to not say “imagine if we had pro players” during his interview while leaving the field with LSU up 31-3 at halftime.

Kiffin, never one to shy away from the drama, was clearly referencing the absence of tight end Dae’Quan Wright and defensive lineman Zxavian Harris, the two ex-NFL training camp participants who LSU sought to add — and won an injunction via a Louisiana judge — but did not get placed on the gameday roster amid an ongoing legal fight with the SEC, which sued LSU in federal court this week.

Notre Dame defensive tackle transfer Junior Tuihalamaka, who also is returning to college for a fifth season amid the NCAA’s age-based eligibility rule change, did suit up for LSU, though. But he did not sign with an NFL team like Harris and Wright did, making him an exception to the rule preventing those two from playing.

After the game, Kiffin didn’t have much to say about the Wright and Harris going forward. The Tigers could still add Wright and Harris later this season, even though they didn’t roster them before Saturday’s game. Kiffin declined to say what (if anything) he’ll do next with them. — Khan and Matt Baker

That might be premature. Season openers are overreaction theater, and it’s possible Clemson just ran into a storm — an LSU team and fan base in a foul mood. The motto on shirt-pins around campus: “Beat everybody.” And it was taken out on Clemson.

But the gap on display Saturday night is unacceptable for Swinney’s program. Clemson and LSU played down to the wire last year, and both finished 7-6. LSU changed coaches and looked like a national title contender. Clemson looked like directional-school fodder.

It doesn’t look good. But it’s also just one game.

Swinney has to get the offense fixed. The Clemson defense was certainly dominated, but it also didn’t have any help, between field position and time on the field. There’s enough talent on defense to win games, if the offense can move the ball.

That looks like a big if. — Seth Emerson

One first down. Fifty-four yards. Three points, via a short field following a tipped interception. That’s all Clemson managed on offense in the first half. The second half, at that point, was irrelevant.

It’s only one game, but the two biggest changes to the offense were a dud.

Vizzina, the senior long expected to be the new starting quarterback, showed why it took until this week to be officially given the job. When Reynolds, a three-star Class of 2026 signee, gave him a push this spring and summer, perhaps it said more about Vizzina than Reynolds. Vizzina, despite having some experience, including one start last year, looked spooked against the LSU pass rush.

Reynolds didn’t look too much better when he replaced Vizzina, late in the first half and into the second half. But Vizzina had more experience and preparation and instead looked like the freshman.

Then there was the decision to bring back Chad Morris as offensive coordinator. This is a long way from 2014, when Morris wrapped up his four-year stint and then left to become SMU’s head coach. Since his disastrous two-year tenure at Arkansas, Morris has bounced around, and this game didn’t make it look like it would be 2014 all over again. — Emerson

LSU came into the season just outside the top 10 in the AP poll, and the Tigers sure looked the part of a top-10 team. Clemson may not be very good based on what we saw, but LSU’s dominance speaks volumes on a day when other ranked teams had their hands full with less talented opposition.

It’s still too early to stamp this team as a one of the five best in the country or lock it into a College Football Playoff berth — after all, there’s still a lot of good teams left on the LSU schedule, including Ole Miss, Texas A&M, Alabama, Texas and Tennessee. LSU entered Saturday night with a 27 percent chance to make the CFP, according to The Athletic’s projections.

But Saturday’s start was promising. The offense produced in all phases. The defense was dominant. And the “Portal King” seems to have hit on most of the key transfers from his No. 1 portal class. This is about as strong a start as LSU fans could have drawn up for the Kiffin era. If Leavitt is healthy, the Tigers will be a problem for SEC teams throughout the 2026 season. At least for today, this absolutely looks like a Playoff team. — Khan

Tiger Stadium was our staff’s clear No. 1 choice as the best stadium in the country last year.

Fans climbed trees and light poles to try to get a look of Kiffin and the Tigers walking into the stadium. The pregame sidelines were packed five-people deep with celebrities (Livvy Dunne), NFL alumni (Justin Jefferson), recruits, other dignitaries and media members.

“Electric,” said LSU fan Rachel LeBoeuf, who sported a button of Kiffin and Ed Orgeron wearing matching sweater vests.

It’s hard to quantify how much the environment mattered, but one early sequence stands out. LSU’s noise helped force Clemson into a false start on second down. On third-and-long, Kiffin waved his arms in the air three times to get fans to yell even louder. His defense snuffed out the rush to force a punt.

The atmosphere Saturday night was Death Valley at its best. — Matt Baker

LSU will be heavily favored at 7:30 p.m. ET next Saturday against Louisiana Tech. The Bulldogs beat FCS foe Northwestern State 80-6 on Saturday, but they haven’t beaten LSU since 1904. Kiffin makes his highly anticipated return to Ole Miss the following Saturday, Sept. 19.

Clemson will play Georgia Southern in its home opener at 7:30 p.m. ET Saturday night before welcoming Bill Belichick and North Carolina on Sept. 19.
